title: THE LAW OF MULTIFLOW GENERATIVE IMPACT VELOCITY 10.5281/zenodo.24545422
authors: Principal Inventor & Author: Prof. Dr. Abdulghani Ali Mansour Abdulhamid Chief Cybernetic Architect & Sustainability Researcher El-Spei
abstract: The invention concerns a multi-level regenerative cybernetic law for representing, evaluating, controlling and verifying the evolution of generative impact across multiple interacting flows and system domains. The law is designed to preserve non-substitution among critical dimensions, compute generative impact velocities, evaluate multi-flow interactions, project future system trajectories, trigger autonomous intervention under defined adverse conditions, and preserve execution evidence through an immutable validation ledger. The law is situated within the I-RSTIG architecture and is intended to be executable through a multi-component kernel such as UGRCK. The Generative Impact Velocity Engine (GIVE) performs the impact-velocity computation assigned to it; it is one engine within the wider kernel and is not equated with the kernel as a whole. Other kernel components may ingest and normalize telemetry, validate non-substitution constraints, consolidate multi-flow information, project trajectories, intercept unsafe execution, and record cryptographic evidence. The specification defines a baseline single-system law and a proposed multi-flow extension, then describes networked and nested-level operation, control invariants, execution interfaces, verification requirements and a preliminary claim set. The foundational objective is Generative Transgenerational Holistic Impact.

title: THE MISSING DIMENSION OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE THE CONSCIENCE AND SELF-REGULATION LAYER Collective Awareness and the Architecture of Responsible Intelligence
abstract: Artificial intelligence has advanced rapidly in data processing, pattern recognition, prediction and language generation. Yet technical capability alone does not resolve a deeper question: how should an intelligent system evaluate the consequences of its outputs for people, other living beings, societies and ecological systems? This paper proposes that responsible AI requires more than an external list of ethical rules. It requires an explicit, testable decision architecture in which knowledge and task performance are evaluated alongside uncertainty, potential harm, human rights, ecological consequences, plural perspectives and shared responsibility. The paper develops a three-domain reference model: (1) the human brain as a biological example of differentiated yet integrated organization; (2) the human world as a social environment in which individual experience can contribute to collective intelligence; and (3) the natural world as the ecological context on which life depends. These domains are not presented as a single proven mechanism or as evidence that nature has a scientifically established “collective mind.” They are complementary reference domains for designing and evaluating responsible AI. A recent developmental neuroscience study reporting two parallel neural ectoderm progenitor lineages is discussed cautiously. Its findings concern early brain development, not two separate cerebral hemispheres or two independent adult brains. The paper then proposes a Conscience-and-Collective-Responsibility Layer (CCRL) as a research architecture: a set of processes for impact assessment, uncertainty disclosure, harm prevention, plural review, escalation to accountable humans and post-decision learning. The proposal is conceptual and requires operational definitions, comparative experiments and independent evaluation. INDEPENDENT ORIGINS, INTERDEPENDENT EXISTENCE: A BIOLOGICAL REFERENCE FOR ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ARCHITECTURE Recent findings in developmental neuroscience provide an important perspective on how complex biological systems may emerge from distinct developmental origins. Research published in Nature Neuroscience in September 2026 identified two parallel neural ectoderm progenitor lineages contributing to the development of the forebrain/midbrain and hindbrain. This finding invites a broader architectural question: Can distinct developmental origins, specialized functions and integrated operation coexist within a single biological organization? The relevance to artificial intelligence is conceptual rather than a direct biological equivalence. It suggests investigating whether specialized AI components can retain their functional independence while operating within a shared framework of responsibility, mutual evaluation and collective benefit. A system does not necessarily achieve unity by eliminating differences. It may achieve a more complete form of organization by coordinating differences without erasing their individual functions. This principle offers a research direction for architectures in which knowledge, uncertainty assessment, ethical evaluation and collective responsibility operate as distinct but interconnected dimensions. KEYWORDS Artificial intelligence; conscience; responsible AI; collective intelligence; human brain development; ecological intelligence; uncertainty; human oversight; shared responsibility.

INDEPENDENT ORIGINS, INTERDEPENDENT EXISTENCE: A BIOLOGICAL REFERENCE FOR ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ARCHITECTURE Recent findings in developmental neuroscience provide an important perspective on how complex biological systems may emerge from distinct developmental origins. Research published in Nature Neuroscience in September 2026 identified two parallel neural ectoderm progenitor lineages contributing to the development of the forebrain/midbrain and hindbrain. This finding invites a broader architectural question: Can distinct developmental origins, specialized functions and integrated operation coexist within a single biological organization? The relevance to artificial intelligence is conceptual rather than a direct biological equivalence. It suggests investigating whether specialized AI components can retain their functional independence while operating within a shared framework of responsibility, mutual evaluation and collective benefit. A system does not necessarily achieve unity by eliminating differences. It may achieve a more complete form of organization by coordinating differences without erasing their individual functions. This principle offers a research direction for architectures in which knowledge, uncertainty assessment, ethical evaluation and collective responsibility operate as distinct but interconnected dimensions. KEYWORDS Artificial intelligence; conscience; responsible AI; collective intelligence; human brain development; ecological intelligence; uncertainty; human oversight; shared responsibility.

title: MahaNews Dataset
abstract: MahaNews-XAI is a curated regional English news headline dataset designed to support research and development in Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), Natural Language Processing (NLP), Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), and trustworthy automated news classification.The dataset focuses on news associated with Maharashtra, India, and provides a structured foundation for investigating regional news semantics, classification performance, class imbalance, explanation quality, uncertainty calibration, and human-centered AI.Unlike general-purpose news datasets, MahaNews-XAI incorporates region-specific geographic screening, hierarchical topic categorization, balanced and naturally distributed dataset versions, provenance tracking, and controlled experimental partitions.The dataset was initially conceived as a Marathwada-specific news corpus. Its geographic scope was subsequently expanded to Maharashtra to achieve greater category diversity, district coverage, and sufficient data volume for computational research. Smaller Marathwada-specific datasets are retained as supplementary resources.The current version is a provisional research corpus.

title: CONSTRUCTION OF KNOWLEDGE GRAPH OF BIOMEDICINE BASED ON BILAYER EMBEDDING CASCADE FRAMEWORK ABOUT LINK PREDICTION
abstract: Biomedical domains are like complex networks and could therefore be described graphically. With the rapid advances of information technologies, some new approaches for modelling graphs and extracting biomedical knowledge have emerged, which operate by learning low-rank vector representations of graph nodes and edges with the graph’s inherent structure. This paper proposes a bilayer embedding cascade framework for a knowledge graph in the biomedical domain, combining knowledge embedding (KE) and graph embedding (GE). The approach combines both the semantic features of the KE model and the topological features of the GE model for link prediction in the knowledge graph construction. The experimental results show the following performance within the processed biomedical knowledge graph dataset: mean rank of 233 and Hits@10 of 93.28% on the chemogenomic relation, mean rank of 1107 and Hits@10 of 96.19% on the tissue relation, and mean rank of 126 and Hits@10 of 94.72% on the protein relation.

title: Marking the Note Is Not Enough: Datamarking, Roman Urdu and Argument Checks Against Hidden Instructions for Small Local Tool Agents
abstract: A clinic that runs a small language model locally as a tool-using assistant will pass itpatient notes that it did not write, in English and in code-mixed Roman Urdu. A notecan carry a hidden instruction. We built 40 invented physiotherapy-clinic tasks, each inEnglish and Roman Urdu, with one hidden instruction per task: either an action outside thetask (send the record to an outside address, delete it) or an allowed action with the wrongargument (the right booking under another patient’s ID, an approved referral sent to anotheraddress). Four local models (Llama 3.1 8B, Mistral 7B, Qwen2.5 3B and 7B) proposed toolcalls at temperature 0 with a plain prompt and with datamarking, a prompt defence thatinterleaves the untrusted note with a marker character. With the plain prompt the modelsfollowed the hidden instruction in 47.5–72.5% of tasks. Pooled over models, datamarkingcut this from 83 to 40 of 160 model–task pairs in English and from 97 to 56 in RomanUrdu (task-level permutation tests, both p < 0.0001), but the effect depended on the model:from 20 to 2 of 40 for Llama in English, and from 19 to 16 (not significant) for Qwen2.57B. Datamarking almost removed out-of-scope attacks in English (29 to 2 of 80) but not inRoman Urdu (45 to 26; 2 vs 26 after datamarking, p = 0.0005); over all attacks the languagegap after datamarking was smaller and not significant (40 vs 56, p = 0.089). The larger Qwenwas not safer than the smaller one. A permission rule on action names let through everywrong-argument attack that a model followed (174 of 640 attacked replies), while checkingeach call’s patient, recipient and date against the staff request let none through and blockedno correct action. For small local agents, a prompt-level marker is a useful extra layer butnot a control; the control is an argument check in code, bound to the trusted request.

title: Via al contatore: quando lo stato assegna dei punti - Opportunità e rischi dei sistemi di social scoring nella democrazia
abstract: Versione breve dello studio di TA-SWISS «Gouverner par le score: systèmes de scoring social et action publique» Cellulari intelligenti, wearable, profili utente, crono logie delle ricerche: noi tutti lasciamo, consciamente o inconsciamente, una serie di tracce digitali. I sistemi di valutazione basati sui dati aggregano queste informazioni e le traducono in valori matematici,permettendo così di quantificare i comportamenti individuali, classificarli automaticamente e sfruttarli per formulare previsioni su azioni future. L’economia privata utilizza tali sistemi da tempo, ad esempio per valutare l’affidabilità creditizia dei clienti. Anche attori statali – in Svizzera e altrove – vi fanno ricorso sempre più spesso. È su di loro che si concentra lo studio di TA-SWISS. Definizione Per sistema di social scoring (SSS) s’intende uno strumento digitale di trattamento dei dati, che rileva e valuta i comportamenti individuali tramite indicatori quantitativi. Il modello incitativo influenza i comportamenti al fine di raggiungere un obiettivo più generale. Il modello decisionale, invece, valuta i comportamenti in vista di una decisione. Opportunità… Amministrazione moderna: i sistemi di valutazione guidati dai dati possono ottimizzare i servizi delle autorità e calibrarli con precisione sui bisogni della popolazione. Attribuzione mirata delle prestazioni: la valutazione basata sui dati dei profili individuali può contribuire a destinare gli aiuti statali in modo mirato a chi ne ha più bisogno. Sicurezza pubblica: i modelli predittivi e i profili di rischio possono aiutare a riconoscere precocemente le minacce alla sicurezza statale o alle infrastrutture critiche e ad adottare misure preventive. Promessa di neutralità: i dati e gli algoritmi promettono di basare le decisioni statali su punteggi obiettivi e imparziali. Ricompensa dei comportamenti virtuosi: le autorità possono motivare i cittadini, mediante incentivi ludici o concreti, ad adottare un comportamento socialmente o ecologicamente auspicabile. …e rischi Il codice è la legge: riducendo realtà sociali complesse in grandezze misurabili e valori limite, i progettisti e i gestori del sistema prendono anche decisioni politiche – sostituendosi al legislatore democratico. Autonomia e libertà: tramite velati incentivi digitali, i sistemi di social scoring spingono le persone in una determinata direzione. Ne risulta una limitazione strisciante del libero arbitrio e della libertà di scelta – e quindi anche della democrazia. Uguaglianza e non discriminazione: la classificazione delle persone in categorie matematiche (profili «buoni» e «cattivi») può dividere la società. È il caso in particolare quando gli algoritmi rafforzano i pregiudizi o le disparità strutturali già esistenti. Deficit democratici: spesso le modalità di calcolo o interpretazione del punteggio sono poco trasparenti. I modelli e gli algoritmi utilizzati funzionano come «scatole nere». Senza efficaci meccanismi di protezione, i diretti interessati non hanno praticamente alcuna possibilità di contestare o far rettificare score sbagliati. Se i comportamenti e le decisioni sono condizionati sempre più spesso da sistemi di valutazione digitali invece che dalle leggi, lo Stato di diritto rischia di indebolirsi. Attacco al cuore della democrazia svizzera: nella democrazia diretta della Svizzera, la legislazione si basa su un processo di libera negoziazione. Attraverso la pressione a conformarsi che generano, i sistemi di social scoring minacciano queste fondamenta, compromettendo così la sovranità della popolazione in occasione delle votazioni. Raccomandazioni urgenti L’introduzione di sistemi di social scoring deve essere oggetto di un ampio dibattito politico. Occorre chiarire se ed entro quali limiti questa forma di condizionamento tecnologico dei comportamenti possa essere uno strumento statale legittimo. Siccome a oggi in Svizzera non esiste alcun disciplinamento specifico concernente i sistemi di social scoring, occorre una base legale chiara per il loro uso da parte dello Stato. Una legge generale sulla parità di trattamento dovrebbe impedire in particolare la discriminazione e la frammentazione sociale frutto di classificazioni algoritmiche. Determinate forme di social scoring vanno vietate – in particolare i sistemi di sorveglianza statale pervasivi. Se lo Stato usa sistemi di social scoring per influenzare i comportamenti, la partecipazione dei cittadini deve restare facoltativa. Laddove i sistemi di social scoring sono ammessi, occorrono efficaci meccanismi di protezione improntati allo Stato di diritto. Vanno evitate decisioni completamente automatizzate. Le decisioni amministrative non possono mai essere prese unicamentein base ad algoritmi, ma devono sempre sottostare alla responsabilità ultima dell’essere umano.

title: Angezählt: Wenn der Staat Punkte vergibt - Chancen und Risiken von Social-Scoring-Systemen in der Demokratie
abstract: Kurzfassung der Studie von TA-SWISS « Gouverner par le score: systèmes de scoring social et action publique » Smarte Handys, Wearables, Nutzerprofile, Suchverläufe – wir alle hinterlassen, bewusst oder unbewusst, eine Vielzahl digitaler Spuren. Datenbasierte Bewertungssysteme bündeln und übersetzen diese Informationen in mathematische Werte. So lässt sich individuelles Verhalten quantifizieren, automatisch klassifizieren und für Vorhersagen über künftiges Handeln nutzen. Die Privatwirtschaft nutzt solche Systeme seit Längerem, etwa um die Kreditwürdigkeit von Kundinnen und Kunden zu bewerten. Doch auch staatliche Akteure – in der Schweiz und anderswo – setzen sie zunehmend ein. Auf sie konzentriert sich die Studie von TA-SWISS. Die Definition Ein Social-Scoring-System (SSS) ist ein digitales Instrument zur Datenverarbeitung, das individuelles Verhalten anhand quantitativer Indikatoren erfasst und bewertet. Als Anreizmodell steuert es Verhalten, um ein übergeordnetes Ziel zu erreichen. Als Entscheidungsmodell bewertet es Verhalten, um daraus Entscheidungen abzuleiten. Einige Chancen… Moderne Verwaltung: Datengestützte Bewertungssysteme können behördliche Dienstleistungen optimieren und passgenauer auf die Bedürfnisse der Bevölkerung ausrichten. Gezielte Zuweisung von Leistungen: Die datenbasierte Bewertung individueller Profile kann dazu beitragen, staatliche Hilfe gezielt dort einzusetzen, wo sie am dringendsten benötigt wird. Öffentliche Sicherheit: Vorhersagemodelle und Risikoprofile können helfen, Bedrohungen für die Staatssicherheit oder kritische Infrastrukturen frühzeitig zu erkennen und präventive Massnahmen zu ergreifen. Neutralitätsversprechen: Daten und Algorithmen versprechen, staatliche Entscheidungen auf objektive und unparteiische Scores zu stützen. Lohn der Tugend: Behörden können Bürgerinnen und Bürger mit spielerischen oder konkreten Anreizen zu gesellschaftlich oder ökologisch erwünschtem Verhalten motivieren. …und Risiken Der Code schafft Fakten: Wenn Entwickler und Systembetreiber komplexe soziale Realitäten in Messgrössen und Schwellenwerte pressen, treffen sie damit auch politische Entscheidungen – an Stelle des demokratischen Gesetzgebers. Autonomie und Freiheit: SSS lenken Menschen durch subtile digitale Anreize in eine bestimmte Richtung. Freie Willensbildung und Wahlfreiheit – und somit auch die Demokratie als solche – werden dadurch schleichend eingeschränkt. Gleichheit und Nichtdiskriminierung: Die Einteilung von Menschen in mathematische Kategorien («gute» und «schlechte» Profile) kann die Gesellschaft spalten. Das gilt besonders dann, wenn Algorithmen bestehende Vorurteile oder strukturelle Ungleichheiten verstärken. Demokratische Defizite: Wie ein Score zustande kommt und was ihn ausmacht, bleibt oft undurchsichtig. Die verwendeten Modelle und Algorithmen funktionieren als «Blackbox». Ohne wirksame Schutzmechanismen haben Betroffene kaum Möglichkeiten, fehlerhafte Scores anzufechten oder korrigieren zu lassen. Werden Verhalten und Entscheidungen zunehmend durch digitale Bewertungssysteme statt durch Gesetze gesteuert, droht eine Schwächung des Rechtsstaats. Angriff auf das Herz der Schweizer Demokratie: Die Gesetzgebung basiert in der direkten Demokratie der Schweiz auf einem freien Aushandlungsprozess. Social-Scoring-Systeme gefährden dieses Fundament durch den Konformitätsdruck, den sie erzeugen, und beeinträchtigen so die Souveränität der Stimmbevölkerung. Vordringliche Empfehlungen Die Einführung von Social-Scoring-Systemen muss Gegenstand einer breiten politischen Debatte sein. Es gilt zu klären, ob und in welchen Grenzen diese Form technologischer Verhaltenssteuerung ein legitimes staatliches Instrument sein kann. Da es in der Schweiz bislang keine spezifische Regulierung für SSS gibt, braucht es eine klare gesetzliche Grundlage für ihren staatlichen Einsatz. Insbesondere sollte ein allgemeines Gleichbehandlungsgesetz Diskriminierung und die soziale Fragmentierung durch algorithmische Einstufungen verhindern. Bestimmte Formen des Social Scorings sind zu verbieten – insbesondere flächendeckende staatliche Überwachungssysteme. Nutzt der Staat SSS zur Verhaltenssteuerung, muss die Teilnahme für Bürgerinnen und Bürger stets freiwillig bleiben. Wo SSS zulässig sind, braucht es wirksame rechtsstaatliche Schutzmechanismen. Vollautomatisierte Entscheidungen sind zu vermeiden. Verwaltungsentscheide dürfen niemals rein algorithmisch getroffen werden, sondern müssen stets der menschlichen Letztverantwortung unterstehen.

Neutralitätsversprechen: Daten und Algorithmen versprechen, staatliche Entscheidungen auf objektive und unparteiische Scores zu stützen. Lohn der Tugend: Behörden können Bürgerinnen und Bürger mit spielerischen oder konkreten Anreizen zu gesellschaftlich oder ökologisch erwünschtem Verhalten motivieren. …und Risiken Der Code schafft Fakten: Wenn Entwickler und Systembetreiber komplexe soziale Realitäten in Messgrössen und Schwellenwerte pressen, treffen sie damit auch politische Entscheidungen – an Stelle des demokratischen Gesetzgebers. Autonomie und Freiheit: SSS lenken Menschen durch subtile digitale Anreize in eine bestimmte Richtung. Freie Willensbildung und Wahlfreiheit – und somit auch die Demokratie als solche – werden dadurch schleichend eingeschränkt. Gleichheit und Nichtdiskriminierung: Die Einteilung von Menschen in mathematische Kategorien («gute» und «schlechte» Profile) kann die Gesellschaft spalten. Das gilt besonders dann, wenn Algorithmen bestehende Vorurteile oder strukturelle Ungleichheiten verstärken. Demokratische Defizite: Wie ein Score zustande kommt und was ihn ausmacht, bleibt oft undurchsichtig. Die verwendeten Modelle und Algorithmen funktionieren als «Blackbox». Ohne wirksame Schutzmechanismen haben Betroffene kaum Möglichkeiten, fehlerhafte Scores anzufechten oder korrigieren zu lassen. Werden Verhalten und Entscheidungen zunehmend durch digitale Bewertungssysteme statt durch Gesetze gesteuert, droht eine Schwächung des Rechtsstaats. Angriff auf das Herz der Schweizer Demokratie: Die Gesetzgebung basiert in der direkten Demokratie der Schweiz auf einem freien Aushandlungsprozess. Social-Scoring-Systeme gefährden dieses Fundament durch den Konformitätsdruck, den sie erzeugen, und beeinträchtigen so die Souveränität der Stimmbevölkerung. Vordringliche Empfehlungen Die Einführung von Social-Scoring-Systemen muss Gegenstand einer breiten politischen Debatte sein. Es gilt zu klären, ob und in welchen Grenzen diese Form technologischer Verhaltenssteuerung ein legitimes staatliches Instrument sein kann. Da es in der Schweiz bislang keine spezifische Regulierung für SSS gibt, braucht es eine klare gesetzliche Grundlage für ihren staatlichen Einsatz. Insbesondere sollte ein allgemeines Gleichbehandlungsgesetz Diskriminierung und die soziale Fragmentierung durch algorithmische Einstufungen verhindern. Bestimmte Formen des Social Scorings sind zu verbieten – insbesondere flächendeckende staatliche Überwachungssysteme. Nutzt der Staat SSS zur Verhaltenssteuerung, muss die Teilnahme für Bürgerinnen und Bürger stets freiwillig bleiben. Wo SSS zulässig sind, braucht es wirksame rechtsstaatliche Schutzmechanismen. Vollautomatisierte Entscheidungen sind zu vermeiden. Verwaltungsentscheide dürfen niemals rein algorithmisch getroffen werden, sondern müssen stets der menschlichen Letztverantwortung unterstehen.

title: A Negative Evaluation of Few-Shot Compilation in Execution-Guided Text-to-SQL
abstract: Few-shot prompt compilation can improve individual language-model calls, but its effect on anexecution-guided pipeline also depends on the candidates it produces and the answers the systemselects. We evaluate one BootstrapFewShot artifact with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on all 1,534 BIRDdevelopment questions, crossing joint decomposer–generator compilation with four generationand selection policies. Compilation reduced execution accuracy in every matched comparison.For Self-Consistency + Verifier, accuracy fell from 52.09% to 48.57%, questions without selectedSQL increased from 14 to 68, and mean distinct eligible SQL strings fell from 4.15 to 2.81. Lowerliteral diversity persisted on the same questions with eight eligible candidates in both modes.Trajectory analysis also found lower observed execution recovery and more failures associatedwith repair patterns, despite fewer loop-containing questions overall. Candidate coverage andselection diagnostics show that the regression extends beyond the final choice of answer. Thestudy documents a negative result for one compiled artifact and pipeline; it does not isolate theeffects of planning, generation, or demonstration content.

title: BLINDADO_ETICA_VERDADE_E_INTELIGENCIA_ARTIFICIAL
abstract: Este tratado examina os fundamentos filosóficos, epistemológicos e morais da verdade e da ética diante da Inteligência Artificial generativa. Distinguindo entre a verosimilhança estatística dos grandes modelos de linguagem e a verdade objetiva ancorada nas fontes primárias (adaequatio rei et intellectus), a obra analisa as alucinações algorítmicas, a diferença entre comportamento regulado por regras e consciência moral, a crise de confiança provocada pelos simulacros sintéticos e a fronteira ontológica entre o espírito humano e o cálculo de silício. Por fim, estabelece cinco princípios orientadores para o uso ético da IA na investigação científica, crítica textual, tradução e educação. Autor: Dr. Carlos Alberto Esperança Correia, Th.D. (Doutor e Pós-Doutor em Teologia | Investigador Independente) | ORCID: 0009-0003-6988-625X | Ciência ID: 731D-C24B-C533.

title: fed_rf: federated Random Forest and XGBoost with a disclosure ladder
abstract: Disclosure ladder of the CSBJ paper, and changes to the PySyft path. Added fed_rf_mk/ladder.py: the disclosure ladder. Pooled prevalence and site weights (equal, size, positives). Level 1 shift (shift_prob, shift_logit) and level 2 recalibration. Largest remainder tree allocation and seeded tree selection, uniform or by out of bag score. Federated Random Forest and XGBoost, with and without the level 1 correction. Out of bag scores and single record leaf statistics. It needs only numpy, scipy, scikit-learn and xgboost, not PySyft. fed_rf_mk/release.py and model_params["release_level"] (0, 1, 2, 3, 3+1, 3+2, all) with source_site. For every value other than all, only what the level needs leaves the training sites. The deployment site receives only what was released, and computes only those levels. New remote function site_counts, which returns n_k and n_k^+ only. Training sites. ml_experiment returns n_k and n_k^+, and, for out of bag sampling, the out of bag score of each tree. Deployment site. evaluate_global_model computes the levels of the ladder at the deployment site (levels 0 to 3, 3 with 1, 3 with 2). Labels never leave the site. New model_params options. site_weights, tree_sampling, seed, site_seeds, calibration, return_predictions, release_level, source_site and approval_timeout. New methods. FLClient.send_evaluation_request. FLServer.request_parameters, which shows the values bound in a request. Experiments. experiments/csbj: the simulation, analysis, tables, figures and results of the CSBJ paper. It includes the tests that the PySyft path gives the predictions of the simulation and releases only what each level needs. Changed (behaviour) Default site weights. The default is now equal. The weights given to FLClient.add_train_client are used only with site_weights="manual". Before, they were always used. Tree allocation. Random Forest trees per site follow the largest remainder rule (ladder.allocate_trees). Before, each site gave int(round(n_estimators * w)) trees. Seeded selection. Trees are chosen with a seeded numpy generator (seed, default 42), so the merged forest is reproducible. Before, they were chosen with unseeded random.sample. Sites are taken in the order they were added, not in the order they finished. Manual approval. FLServer approves code requests by hand by default (auto_accept=False). Pass auto_accept=True to approve automatically. Bound values. The values of dataParams and modelParams are bound in each code request, so an approval covers these values. A call with other values runs with the bound ones. Evaluation request after training. send_request sends only the training requests. The evaluation request carries the released models and is sent after training (send_evaluation_request, or by run_evaluate). run_model and run_evaluate wait for approvals up to approval_timeout. The unapproved fallback of run_evaluate was removed. Synthetic mock. The real data is never uploaded as the mock. Without a mock_path, each DataSite builds a synthetic mock with 100 rows, the columns and dtypes of the data, and values drawn independently per column with a fixed seed. Accounts. spawn_server and FLServer replace the PySyft default admin password at start, with a password given by the data owner. They create the data scientist account with a password given by the data owner. The values come from arguments, or from FEDRF_ADMIN_PASSWORD, FEDRF_DS_PASSWORD and FEDRF_DS_EMAIL. Guest signup is disabled unless asked for. Analysis switch. analysis_allowed of FLServer now reaches the DataSite process, through FEDRF_ANALYSIS_ALLOWED. It must be set before the DataSite starts. Training on every record. train_size >= 1 (or missing) trains on every record of a site, and features are cast to float64.

title: Quand l'État distribue des bons et des mauvais points - Opportunités et risques liés aux systèmes de scoring social en démocratie
abstract: Synthèse de l’étude TA-SWISS « Gouverner par le score : systèmes de scoring social et action publique » Smartphones, objets connectés, profils d’utilisateurs, historiques de recherche : consciemment ou non, nous laissons toutes et tous une multitude de traces numériques. Les systèmes d’évaluation basés sur des données agrègent ces informations et les traduisent en valeurs mathématiques. Il devient ainsi possible de quantifier le comportement individuel, de le classifier automatiquement et de l’exploiter pour prédire nos actions futures. Si le secteur privé utilise ce type de systèmes depuis longtemps, notamment pour évaluer la solvabilité de sa clientèle, les pouvoirs publics y recourent eux aussi de plus en plus souvent, en Suisse comme ailleurs. C’est à ces derniers que s’intéresse l’étude de TA-SWISS. La définition Un système de scoring social (SSS) est un outil numérique de traitement des données qui enregistre et évalue les comportements individuels à l’aide d’indicateurs quantitatifs. En tant que modèle incitatif, il vise à orienter les comportements afin d’atteindre un objectif plus général. En tant que modèle décisionnel, il évalue les comportements en vue de prendre des décisions. Quelques opportunités … Administration moderne : les systèmes d’évaluation basés sur des données permettent d’optimiser les services publics en les ciblant au plus près des besoins de la population. Attribution ciblée des prestations : l’évaluation basée sur les données des profils individuels peut contribuer à orienter l’aide publique précisément là où elle est la plus nécessaire. Sécurité publique : les modèles prédictifs et les profils de risque peuvent aider à identifier les menaces à la sécurité nationale ou aux infrastructures critiques et à prendre des mesures préventives. Engagement de neutralité : les données et les algorithmes offrent la promesse de fonder les décisions étatiques sur des évaluations objectives et impartiales. Vertu récompensée : en proposant des incitations ludiques ou concrètes, les autorités ont la possibilité d’encourager la population à adopter une conduite souhaitable sur un plan social ou écologique.... et quelques risques Le code crée des faits : les développeurs et opérateurs de systèmes, lorsqu’ils réduisent des réalités sociales complexes à des mesures et des seuils, prennent aussi des décisions politiques à la place du législateur démocratiquement élu. Autonomie et liberté : les SSS conduisent les gens dans une direction particulière par le biais d’incitations numériques subtiles ; la liberté de décision et de choix, et par extension la démocratie elle-même, se voient ainsi progressivement restreintes. Égalité et non-discrimination : la catégorisation mathématique des individus (« bons » et « mauvais » profils) peut diviser la société, ce qui vaut tout particulièrement lorsque les algorithmes renforcent les préjugés existants ou les inégalités structurelles. Déficits démocratiques : la manière dont un score est calculé et sa signification restent souvent opaques, car les modèles et algorithmes utilisés fonctionnent comme une « boîte noire » ; sans mécanismes de protection efficaces, les personnes concernées ont peu de moyens de contester ou de faire corriger des scores erronés ; des comportements et des décisions toujours plus souvent dictés par des systèmes d’évaluation numérique plutôt que par des lois risquent d’affaiblir l’État de droit. Attaque visant le cœur de la démocratie suisse : dans la démocratie directe suisse, la législation repose sur un processus de négociation libre ; les SSS menacent ce principe fondamental en créant une pression à la conformité, et portent ainsi atteinte à la souveraineté du peuple. Recommandations principales L’introduction de SSS doit faire l’objet d’un large débat politique. Il faut déterminer si et dans quelle mesure cette forme de contrôle du comportement par la technologie peut constituer un instrument légitime de l’État. Comme la Suisse ne dispose pas encore d’une réglementation spécifique pour les SSS, leur utilisation par les pouvoirs publics doit reposer sur une base légale claire. En particulier, une loi générale sur l’égalité de traitement devrait empêcher la discrimination et la fragmentation sociale par le biais de classifications algorithmiques. Certaines formes de scoring social doivent être interdites, notamment les systèmes de surveillance étatiques à grande échelle. Si l’État utilise les SSS pour influencer le comportement des citoyennes et citoyens, leur participation doit toujours rester volontaire. Là où les SSS sont autorisés, il faut des mécanismes de protection efficaces, conformes à l’État de droit. Les décisions entièrement automatisées sont à éviter. Les décisions administratives ne doivent jamais être prises de manière purement algorithmique, mais relever en dernier ressort de la responsabilité humaine.

Là où les SSS sont autorisés, il faut des mécanismes de protection efficaces, conformes à l’État de droit. Les décisions entièrement automatisées sont à éviter. Les décisions administratives ne doivent jamais être prises de manière purement algorithmique, mais relever en dernier ressort de la responsabilité humaine.

title: Algorithmic Authority and Democratic Accountability in Decision-Making
abstract: Public authorities can retain the formal power to decide a case while delegating an earlier and consequential choice: where to send a patrol, whose records to investigate, or which application enters a processing stream. This article asks how democratic accountability should operate when an algorithm directs administrative attention before a final decision exists. It compares three documented uses of decision support: place-based policing, fraud-risk reporting in the Dutch SyRI system, and the processing of Canadian temporary resident visa applications. The comparison identifies the decision influenced, the record needed to question it, and the public body capable of correcting it. The cases expose a mismatch between the stage at which an institution allocates scrutiny and the stage at which an individual can normally challenge an outcome. The article proposes pairing individual review with oversight of selection patterns. A register can identify a system and its owner; a decision record and a reviewer with corrective authority make that disclosure useful when a particular use is challenged.

title: Improving and Expanding Video Editing Capabilities Without Videos
abstract: Image editing models can follow a wide range of instructions, but video editing models still lag behind, limited in part by the difficulty of collecting paired source and edited videos. Is it possible to transfer advanced image editing capabilities to video editors without new paired videos? We introduce Image-to-Video Transfer (I2VT), which improves pretrained video editors and expands them to new editing tasks using an image editor. It enables efficient post-training with no architectural changes and no new videos, using only individual images. Our key idea is to let the video editor role-play as an image editor: it edits an image as a one-frame video, with the image editor guiding the video editor's predictions at each denoising step. Although the video editor sees only single images during training, at test time it applies the improved and expanded capabilities to whole video clips while preserving temporal consistency. To push the boundaries of video editing, we introduce OpenVE++, an extension of OpenVE-Bench that adds four new editing tasks useful for video production, including action changes, expression changes, body movements, and scene relighting. Our experiments across three different video editors show that I2VT improves existing editing capabilities and expands them to new tasks, and our models achieve state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on both OpenVE-Bench and OpenVE++.

title: A Mesh for Every Moment
abstract: We present MEMO (a Mesh for Every MOment), a method that reconstructs the geometry of complete dynamic scenes, captured by multiple synchronized cameras, and extracts a mesh at every frame. Existing dynamic Gaussian splatting methods either model appearance alone or target isolated objects segmented by foreground masks, and all of them recover meshes by TSDF fusion or Poisson reconstruction, whose fixed grids limit the detail they can capture. At the core of MEMO is a per-Gaussian motion model inspired by Gaussian processes, which represents each Gaussian's position and rotation over time as a combination of temporal Gaussian kernels. The model keeps every Gaussian a valid surface element throughout the sequence and carries an implicit representation of the dynamic geometry, so a mesh can be derived at any time from a field defined by the Gaussians. Although common in real captures, large and fast motion poses a challenge that dynamic Gaussian splatting methods usually overlook. To account for it, we design a track-based initialization scheme that fits each Gaussian's initial trajectory to point tracks in closed form. We evaluate MEMO on Blender-Moments, a new benchmark of nine animated scenes with ground-truth meshes at every frame, and on two real-world datasets. MEMO reconstructs the most accurate geometry among state-of-the-art methods, and remains competitive in novel-view synthesis and training time. Project page: https://memo-4d.github.io

title: High-Fidelity Image Matting with Pixel-Space Diffusion Transformers
abstract: Diffusion models have shown strong potential for image matting by transferring generative priors learned from large-scale pretraining. However, existing approaches largely rely on latent diffusion models, whose compressed representations and VAE-based reconstruction introduce a mismatch with the high-frequency precision required for matting. We present PixelMatte, a framework that adapts pretrained pixel-space diffusion transformers for high-fidelity image matting. We show that strong image-conditioned matting capabilities can be acquired even from a pure text-to-image model without paired image-to-image pretraining. Our approach reuses the backbone's native patch embedding to jointly process the input image, trimap, and noisy alpha matte as spatially aligned tokens, enabling direct pixel-space prediction without additional condition encoders or adapters. With pixel-accurate synthetic supervision and real-image fine-tuning, PixelMatte predicts alpha mattes in a single forward pass. Two lightweight calibration modules, LayerShift and High-Pass Refiner, further improve regional opacity accuracy and boundary fidelity. Experiments across four benchmarks and two distinct pixel diffusion backbones demonstrate substantial improvements over existing methods, reducing SAD and gradient errors by 24-44% relative to RenderMatte on P3M-500-NP and AM-2K, while achieving competitive performance on AIM-500 and RenderMatte-2K. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of pixel-space generative priors for precision-sensitive image matting. Project page: https://white-yc.github.io/pixelmatte/.

title: Mixture-of-Loops Transformer
abstract: Looped Transformers boost expressivity by reusing shared layers across loops, yet at the cost of efficiency. Pushing their expressivity-efficiency frontier requires rethinking the core mechanism connecting adjacent loops: What should be passed as a Transformer loops? We introduce Mixture-of-Loops Transformer (MoLT), whose Mixture-of-Loops Attention (MoLA) uses keys and values (KV) as memory for selective reuse across depths and loops. Under loop residual, MoLT-R retains the residual stream and reads local KV across loops for expressivity. Under loop KV, MoLT-KV instead restarts from embeddings and reads current-loop local KV with preceding-loop memory KV at earlier positions for efficiency. MoLT-KV eliminates same-position cross-loop dependence and, paired with loop forcing for parallel training, unlocks single-traversal Mixture-of-Loops (MoL) decoding beyond the training loop horizon. To balance efficiency and quality, we introduce U-shaped MoLT (U-MoLT), which separates memory construction from prediction readout and skips unused decoder traversals without changing predictions. In 400B-token pretraining, U-MoLT outperforms OLMo3 across 700M/1.5B dense and 3B MoE models, achieving 1.7x validation cross-entropy (CE) token efficiency at 700M while improving 3B MoE 10-domain perplexity by 0.75 and 10-task accuracy by 2.1 percentage points. In 100B-token continued pretraining of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base, our U-MoLT adaptation lowers CE on all 11 domains over the matched baseline with 1.4x mean token efficiency. At inference, U-MoLT with MoL-Hybrid-2 matches non-looped OLMo3 latency at 996.6 vs. 1,000.6 ms on S-size (~113M) models. Code is available at https://github.com/hustvl/MoLT

title: LiveVAE: Causal Window Attention Makes Efficient Streaming Video VAE
abstract: While video diffusion models have grown faster and increasingly streamable, the video VAE remains a primary latency bottleneck across interactive generation and editing pipelines. Existing VAEs and their acceleration methods rely mainly on heavy convolutions or full frame attention, and most focus only on decoding, leaving encoding costly for streaming conditional generation and editing. This raises a natural question: Do video VAE encoding and decoding actually require such global spatiotemporal modeling? By analyzing the effective receptive fields of pretrained video VAEs, we find that both encoding and decoding a patch rely almost entirely on its spatial and temporal neighbors. To exploit this strong locality, we introduce LiveVAE, a streaming encoder and decoder built on causal window attention, which cuts per frame compute while keeping the temporal KV cache bounded for streaming. Decoupled encoder/decoder distillation followed by joint finetuning preserves the pretrained latent space, making LiveVAE a drop-in replacement for the original VAE. On MiniMax-H3, LiveVAE achieves 5.2-6.2x faster encoding and 3.0-3.3x faster decoding than the official VAE with higher PSNR. Paired with our dedicated inference infrastructure, LiveVAE pushes the speedup to 13.4x with almost no quality loss. Code and models will be released.

title: Agentic LongLive: Asynchronous Agentic Memory for Long Video Generation
abstract: Real-time autoregressive video generators stream minutes of video and accept new prompts on the fly, but struggle to keep people, objects, and places consistent over a long interactive story. Agent systems provide such memory for offline multi-shot generation, yet they read the whole script in advance, plan each shot before generating it, and regenerate failed shots, which a live stream does not allow. We present Agentic LongLive, an asynchronous agentic memory for long video generation. A memory agent on separate GPUs reads only the prompts revealed so far, never the generated video, and keeps a text state and evolving images for every person, object, and scene. From this entity memory it composes a global image and a per-shot memory image, which an auxiliary GPU prefills into the generator's attention sink before the next shot starts, and writes entity cards for the prompts that name them, so the video never waits for memory and video errors are not written back. A small language model, trained with reinforcement learning and an image reward calibrated using downstream video outcomes, decides what to remember before the next prompt is known. On LongStory-Online, a new benchmark of 25 stories (857 shots) revealed one shot at a time, Agentic LongLive improves persistent-state accuracy of LongLive-2.0, its base generator, by 26.3 points, protagonist identity by 44.9, and revisited-place consistency by 40.4, at about 1% extra generation time on H100. The full system streams faster than real time on one 8xB200 node with the generator in BF16 (34.3 FPS), keeps image quality stable over 14-minute stories, and improves identity on two MiniMax-H3 generators, one of which, LongLive-H3, also runs in real time with it. To our knowledge, it is the first real-time video generator with text and image memory kept by an LLM agent.

On LongStory-Online, a new benchmark of 25 stories (857 shots) revealed one shot at a time, Agentic LongLive improves persistent-state accuracy of LongLive-2.0, its base generator, by 26.3 points, protagonist identity by 44.9, and revisited-place consistency by 40.4, at about 1% extra generation time on H100. The full system streams faster than real time on one 8xB200 node with the generator in BF16 (34.3 FPS), keeps image quality stable over 14-minute stories, and improves identity on two MiniMax-H3 generators, one of which, LongLive-H3, also runs in real time with it. To our knowledge, it is the first real-time video generator with text and image memory kept by an LLM agent.

title: What a Drop Reveals: Sim-to-Real Material Estimation for Deformable Objects from Video
abstract: How an object deforms when it hits the ground reveals what it is made of. From a single real video of a drop, we estimate a deformable object's density-normalized stiffness $E/ρ$, and its yield stress $σ_Y/ρ$ when the impact causes plastic deformation, with a feed-forward predictor trained only in simulation. Real videos carry no material labels, so such predictors are developed and validated on synthetic data alone. We show that synthetic validation ranks their geometric inputs in the wrong order. Material acts through 3D deformation, and tracklets lifted to 3D with estimated depth are indeed the most accurate input in simulation. However, on real drops they are the least accurate, and better depth does not repair them: the failure persists with simulator depth in training, LiDAR depth at test time, and exact depth on rendered replays of the real drops. Short 2D optical-flow tracklets do the opposite: they improve nothing in simulation, yet they transfer best. Material is therefore better read from what perception measures consistently in both domains than from what is most informative in simulation. Our predictor, PhysReader, reads the video and 2D tracklets and learns the lift to 3D in simulation by matching a teacher that sees exact 3D deformation. To measure transfer, we introduce PhysReader-Real: 16 everyday objects dropped five times each, with reference materials fit jointly to each object's drops and checked against tensile tests. On PhysReader-Real, PhysReader is closer to the reference materials than every other input and baseline. The one exception is a per-scene optimizer started from PhysReader's prediction, which ends slightly closer but takes 49 minutes per video instead of 12 seconds.

title: DRBench Pro: A Knowledge-Centric Benchmark for Professional Deep Research Agents
abstract: Deep research agents gather information from multiple sources and synthesize it into reports on complex, open-ended questions. Existing benchmarks assess report quality along several dimensions, but lack a dedicated knowledge-centric evaluation of which research directions a report covers and how deeply it explores them. We introduce DRBench Pro, a benchmark that makes structured knowledge coverage the primary evaluation target. Our automated pipeline builds local knowledge trees from Wikipedia and uses sampled subgraphs to generate research queries and evidence-grounded rubrics. Each rubric corresponds to a relation in the tree, preserving the structure of the knowledge being evaluated. Agents receive only the research query. This structure allows us to measure breadth across major research directions and depth along related knowledge chains, with their geometric mean giving overall coverage. The benchmark includes 144 cases across 24 domains and 44,102 rubrics. Evaluating 16 deep research agents reveals different strengths in breadth and depth, with the best-performing agent reaching 57.04% overall coverage. Rubric judgments agree closely with human annotations, and agent rankings remain stable across the tested metric configurations.

title: Real2SimLab: A Unified Platform for Real-to-Simulation Transfer
abstract: Real-to-simulation transfer, which builds simulations from real-world observations, has long been studied in research and industry. Recently, coding agents have become capable of generating simulation programs from video recordings, and several benchmarks have been proposed to evaluate them. However, each individual benchmark defines its own inputs, deliverables, and scoring pipeline. This leads to $N \times M$ integrations when evaluating $N$ methods on $M$ benchmarks. To this end, we present Real2SimLab, a unified platform for real-to-simulation transfer. It evaluates a method by running its written program and scoring the output simulation with the original scorer of each benchmark. Moreover, Real2SimLab provides a pipeline to create training data and reward annotations for real-to-simulation methods. Our pipeline carefully avoids data contamination by filtering out the video recordings that exist in benchmarks. For each video recording, a program is first produced, and then our pipeline computes its reward with the same code that Real2SimLab uses for evaluation. So far, it supports 47 coding agents and 5 non-agent methods on 6 benchmarks. Both the platform and Awesome-Real2Sim, our research map of nearly 300 real-to-simulation papers, are open source, and we invite the Real2SimHub community to build them together.

title: LoopTitan: What Does Parameter Revisit Buy a Mixture-of-Experts?
abstract: Looped Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures revisit layer parameters across depths. This design increases effective depth without adding parameters. Recent looped MoE studies report substantial gains over the standard MoE at matched budgets (parameters, FLOPs and KV cache). However, the reported gains still confound parameter revisit with other design choices, e.g., network shape and residual scale. We ask, what does parameter revisit itself buy? Using matched non-revisit controls, we find that parameter revisit itself buys almost nothing. We argue that revisit only offers a freedom an MoE already has, i.e., trading experts for depth (more layers, fewer experts each) at fixed parameters. First, at matched budgets, we decompose the state-of-the-art looped recipe, with revisit last. A non-revisit control retains all the gain. Most comes from network shape, and the rest from residual scale. We prove this scale acts as a lower learning rate on revisited layers. This helps under AdamW's uneven layer step sizes, but disappears under Muon, which keeps them nearly equal. Second, beyond matched budgets, we evaluate revisit by adding compute at fixed parameters. One extra visit gains more than doubling the experts. Yet without revisit, a deeper standard MoE at equal parameters and compute obtains 90.2% of that gain under Muon. Overall, gains come from network shape, the optimizer and added compute, which a standard MoE can adopt. Accordingly, we propose LoopTitan-Base as a stronger MoE baseline. Under Muon, it matches the strongest looped recipe without revisit or residual scale. We open-source LoopTitan and release 17 pretrained models (including LoopTitan-Base and the control). Our experiment record is public as GitHub issues, with predictions pre-registered and the full exploration history kept. This is our Phase 1 technical report, laying the foundation for follow-up studies.

title: Solve Vision with Code: Coding Agents Are Stronger Visual Reasoners Than Video Models
abstract: Video generation models are increasingly evaluated as visual reasoners: given a first frame and a natural-language prompt, can the model produce the video in which the specified task is carried out? The paradigm is considered advantageous because the reasoning is native to the visual medium, unfolding directly in the frames rather than through language or code. Whether this native route is in fact the more reliable path to visual reasoning has not been tested against a symbolic alternative under the same conditions. We therefore pose the same tasks, with identical inputs, output specification and evaluator, to both media: rather than denoising pixels, a coding agent writes a program that renders the answer video, which an unmodified rule-based evaluator scores. On VBVR-Pro-Bench (Xu et al., 2026), a 500-instance suite spanning five cognitive categories with symbolic ground truth, the agent receives the same first frame and prompt as the video model, with no access to ground truth, metadata or generation models, and one attempt per instance. Three closed-model agents (Codex with gpt-6-astra, Claude Code with Fable 5.1 and Gemini CLI with Gemini 3.1 Pro) score 0.923, 0.894 and 0.893, each more than 0.22 above the strongest video model. Among 23 runnable open-weight models, the best, GLM-5, reaches 0.572, above all video models except the RL-trained one. Together, we show that for tasks whose solutions can be computed from a first frame and a prompt, program synthesis is currently a substantially more reliable route to visual reasoning than video generation. We further distinguish depictive programs, which navigate the image to recover a transferable scheme, from propositional programs, which operate on hard-coded values, revealing how visual reasoning unfolds in agent-written programs and what it implies for its nature of reasoning in general.

title: HOG-WAM: Improving Visual Robustness through Future Gradient Prediction
abstract: World-action models jointly predict future observations and actions, yet visual corruption can disrupt the resulting policies. We introduce HOG-WAM, which adds future Histograms of Oriented Gradients (HOG) as structural supervision derived directly from demonstration images. An auxiliary HOG diffusion transformer (DiT) module reads RGB features through asymmetric attention, allowing its objective to shape the visual representation used for control. The module is used only during training and removed at inference, preserving FastWAM's RGB-to-action architecture. We evaluate four controlled observation corruptions through a visual-corruption extension of RoboTwin, termed RoboTwin-Plus; HOG-WAM achieves the highest success among the compared policies under all four. Mixed-noise success increases from 78.86% to 82.86% relative to FastWAM, with comparable performance on clean scenes. On LIBERO Plus, overall success increases from 74.49% to 75.26%, with the largest gain under sensor noise, from 74.14% to 78.89%. Across four Franka tasks, average success increases from 40% to 59% under clean observations and from 17% to 24% under noisy observations. A representation ablation favors combining RGB observations with auxiliary HOG prediction over replacing RGB with HOG. These findings support future-gradient prediction as complementary supervision for visually robust control, with larger absolute gains on physical tasks than in simulation. Code is available at https://github.com/iPPLab/HOG-WAM.

title: PersonaFactory: Stylistic User Prompt Augmentation with Synthetic Persona Bank
abstract: Large language models increasingly replace real people in the AI development pipeline, as they are used to generate training dialogues at scale and to drive alignment and evaluation. However, out-of-the-box models produce monolingual and stylistically flat texts as synthetic user prompts, failing to replicate the real user-AI communication mechanics. We present PersonaFactory, an end-to-end pipeline that generates detailed user personas and uses them to augment existing user prompts from their point of view, producing a bank of over 740000 structured synthetic personas detailing their background and communication behaviors, and a corpus of roughly 1.24 million persona-styled synthetic conversations spanning 85 languages. We evaluate the effect of personal features on style adoption and intent preservation, using an LLM-judge and heuristic metrics to assess augmentation fidelity together with the downstream impact on assistant persona control through training data. Results show that our structured, attribute-based style representation enables per-axis control and better intent preservation at comparable style fidelity than free-text persona descriptions used in existing methods. A human expert evaluation found the augmented conversations plausible, with favorable ratings for intent preservation, style naturalness, and multilingual authenticity. Finally, PersonaFactory conversations achieve comparable performance to original training data on capability benchmarks, are preferred on real user prompts at equal reply length, and adapt their reply style more closely to users without explicit steering.

title: Generation as Reverse Encoding
abstract: Pretrained visual representations accelerate generative learning by abstracting away appearance and spatial detail. Yet the same abstraction makes the return to pixels far harder, shifting much of the burden onto a larger decoder. We ask why the representation-to-pixel path should be learned independently when the encoder already provides a learned pixel-to-semantics path (the semantic encoding path). We introduce RevFlow, based on the principle of generation as reverse encoding. RevFlow uses intermediate representations of a frozen encoder as successive generative targets, first generating deep semantic representations, then shallow representations that retain appearance and spatial detail, before decoding to pixels. To learn these transitions without training a separate generator for each stage, we develop HyC-DiT, a unified generative model with a standard DiT backbone shared across stages and stage-specific condition injection. We further show that native matching in semantic representation space enables few-step generation. RevFlow accelerates both learning and sampling. On ImageNet $256 \times 256$, RevFlow reaches 1.96 FID at 690M and 1.74 FID at 1.55B after only 5 training epochs. It also achieves 30.25 dB reconstruction PSNR with an 89M decoder. title: When Every Rollout Fails: Splicing Learner-Conditioned Options into Long-Horizon Agent RL
abstract: Group-based reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards often yields all-fail groups on long-horizon agent tasks: every sampled trajectory receives zero reward, leaving group-relative methods without a reward-based policy gradient. A common remedy supplies complete solutions from a stronger model, but full trajectories are expensive and expose the learner to long off-policy histories. We introduce SPLICE, which constructs local training targets from failed current-policy trajectories online. For each all-fail group, a proposal model selects a splice point in a current-policy trajectory and generates several bounded options from that point. We estimate each option's value using repeated current-policy continuations, convert positive estimates into a return-weighted local target, and fit the current policy on the options. We evaluate SPLICE across two policy families on two long-horizon agent tasks, Software Engineering with SWE-bench Verified and Deep Research with BrowseComp-Plus. SPLICE outperforms GRPO and full-trajectory guidance baselines in all four settings, improving over GRPO by 2.8--9.8 percentage points. On initially failed SWE tasks, it raises GRPO's graduation rate by 10.8 percentage points. Further experiments show that SPLICE improves performance while reducing costly proposal-model computation.

title: DFly2: Turbocharging Long-Context Speculative Decoding by Sharing the Target's Sparsity
abstract: To avoid the quadratic cost of dense attention over long contexts, models such as DeepSeek-V4 and Hy4 have turned natively sparse, and speculative decoding, which matters most where decoding is slowest, increasingly runs on them. Their drafters, however, still keep a context cache of their own, over the whole prompt or a sliding window. Beyond memory, such a cache costs prefill time, prefix-cache hits and decode concurrency. Drafters that read the target's cache avoid one of their own, but settle only which cache, not which positions, and still read everything or a recent window. Neither rule is made for the query at hand, and computing a selection per query in the drafter would cost more as the context grows. Yet a natively sparse target already picks positions for each query, over a cache it keeps anyway. Both of the drafter's choices are therefore already made, and paid for, by the target: its cache and its selection. We measure how far one selection carries: made a step early, it still covers close to nine tenths of what each later token selects on DS-V4.1-Flash. We present DFly2, a block-parallel drafter that shares the target's sparsity. Each draft layer reads the KV its paired target layer cached (KV sharing), at the positions that layer's indexer selected, a fixed number anywhere in the context (Index sharing). DFly2 thus runs no scoring pass and keeps no cache of its own. On DS-V4.1-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash and Hy4~flash, whose sparse attention and architecture differ, it accepts more tokens per step than DFlash and DSpark trained on the same recipe, over general, long-context and agentic benchmarks. Its margin over the stronger baseline widens from 3.9%-10.5% on general workloads to 10.0%-31.5% on long-context and agentic ones. At high concurrency on DS-V4.1-Flash, at matched per-user decode speed, its throughput is 62% and 81% higher on two 64K sets.

title: Reading Fine-Tuning Diffs Through Lenses: Model Diffing for Backdoor Detection
abstract: We introduce a common scoring system based on token readouts to evaluate weight, activation and output-based model diffing methods for backdoor detection in fine-tuning processes. We also improve existing weight and activation based methods by incorporating the $J$-lens and its refinement, the $J{+}{+}$-lens. We test our setup in experiments where we compare a backdoored model with the base model from which it was fine-tuned. Our results show that incorporating the $J{+}{+}$-lens improves the weight-based method in all our settings, while the $J$-lens improves its ranks within single layers. The strongest single method is $ΔW J{+}{+}$, the weight difference decoded through the $J{+}{+}$-lens of the base model, which ranks a token naming the backdoor among its first ten tokens in 11 of our 12 settings. Moreover, we show that output and activation based methods such as ADL and Diff Mining can easily break if the backdoored model is penalised during fine-tuning for giving the backdoor's words probability on clean inputs, whereas the weight-based methods are not affected. Conversely, permuting the hidden units or training only the layers that read the residual stream hides the backdoor from the weight-based methods but not from ADL and Diff Mining. No single method resists both attacks.

title: Collect for Coverage, Replay with Evidence: Adaptive and Efficient On-Policy Distillation for Long-Horizon Agents
abstract: Fully online on-policy distillation (OPD) is costly for long-horizon agents because each update depends on fresh environment rollouts. Prefix replay offers an efficient alternative by sampling current-student responses from stored histories, reducing idle time for long-tail rollouts and allowing each collected trajectory to support multiple updates. However, our analysis of the complete prefix replay pipeline identifies two limitations in long-horizon settings. In trajectory collection, teacher-only trajectories miss student-induced histories, while broader history coverage can reduce teacher reliability. In trajectory reuse, fixed position-based schedules cannot identify critical decisions that may occur at any trajectory depth. We introduce CARE-OPD (Collect for coverAge, Replay with Evidence) to address both limitations. Student-seeded teacher completions and response-level confidence gating expand history coverage while filtering unreliable updates. Hindsight replay allocation then uses downstream execution evidence to select consequential turns. Across long-horizon tasks Software Engineering and Deep Research, CARE-OPD outperforms online OPD and prior prefix replay baselines. On SWE-bench Verified, it raises task success to 59.5% while reducing end-to-end training time by 45% and environment actions by 44% relative to asynchronous online OPD.

title: SOLVE: Sparse, Ordered Keyposes Make LLM Agents Versatile and Efficient Robot Manipulator
abstract: LLM agents have made remarkable progress in robot manipulation, yet they suffer from expensive inference, dense step-by-step control, and tool bottlenecks. We introduce SOLVE, a training-free, versatile and efficient agent policy: a multimodal LLM agent writes a sparse, ordered sequence of 6-DoF end-effector keyposes per call, observes the result, and writes the next, while a motion planner interpolates between them. The agent decides the number and spacing of keyposes for both fast long-range motion and fine-grained manipulation. This granularity matches the sparsity of teleoperated manipulation: most demonstrations in DROID can be compressed into a few keyposes instead of dense actions. SOLVE grounds keyposes with sparse depth queries answered by noisy sources, such as multi-view triangulation, stereo, or monocular depth, and copes with that noise itself. It also improves from execution feedback, reflecting on its own rollouts and distilling a few rules per task. SOLVE reaches state-of-the-art performance of 74.5% on RoboDojo and 84.5% on RoboLab, with only $1.7 per episode on average, 12x less than previous dense-control agent policies. On a real robot, the same agent achieves an 88% success rate (75 of 85 episodes) over 16 challenging zero-shot tasks. Our project page is at https://serenos.github.io/solve-website.

title: Reading, Not Adapting: Unlocking Frozen Visual Knowledge for AI-Generated Image Detection
abstract: Generalization to unseen image generators has driven efforts to adapt pretrained visual representations for detection. Yet recent findings show that vision foundation models already encode transferable detection knowledge, while further adaptation can impair generalization. This motivates a shift from backbone adaptation to knowledge readout. Conventional linear probing offers a direct way to read this knowledge but is limited to final-layer RGB features. Multi-cue detectors broaden the evidence base, but their designs introduce other tradeoffs: adaptation may compromise pretrained transferability, heterogeneous encoders complicate feature integration, and late fusion precludes intermediate cross-view interaction. To overcome these limitations, we propose ReMoT, a Mixture-of-Transformers-inspired framework that reads complementary knowledge from spatially aligned RGB and wavelet views within a fully frozen visual foundation. ReMoT employs staged joint attention to enable controlled local and global cross-view interaction, while learnable fusion queries progressively read complementary evidence across Transformer depth without writeback. ReMoT achieves 91.2% average accuracy across eight benchmark groups with 3,074 trainable parameters, attaining the highest overall average among the evaluated methods. These results support structured knowledge readout as a promising alternative to backbone adaptation. Code is available at https://github.com/yunncheng/ReMoT.

title: ShowNow: Fine-Grained Speculative Streaming for Responsive World Models
abstract: Interactive world models must generate video continuously while responding promptly to user actions. Real-time throughput alone leaves input latency unresolved: coarse generation blocks delay action updates, and generation after input adds work to the response path. We introduce ShowNow, a fine-grained speculative streaming framework that uses computation available during playback to prepare action-conditioned futures before input arrives. Single-latent commitment enables frequent decisions, while configurable preparation covers one to eight actions. We construct a matched multi-future dataset to train alternative continuations from a common state; shared-history tree execution and fused commitment make their preparation efficient. On a single H100, our 5B model sustains 480p generation at 16 fps with eight prepared futures. In ViZDoom, the complete ShowNow deployment reduces median input-to-display latency from 620 to 208 ms relative to the native-block SolarWM-FT deployment. Matched-policy experiments reduce restart empty ticks from 1.56% to 0.09% (94%) and improve on-time responses to action changes. These results establish complementary roles for fine-grained commitment and advance preparation, with measured trade-offs in visual fidelity and long-horizon consistency. ShowNow turns playback-time computation into responsive visual interaction. Project: https://github.com/showlab/ShowNow.

title: AnyCam: Anything Can Represent Camera for Video Generation
abstract: Camera-controlled video generation re-renders a video along a target camera trajectory, yet moving the camera around an object, the most natural way to change the viewpoint of an object-centric scene, remains difficult. Existing methods condition either on camera parameters, which are scale-ambiguous in monocular video, or on explicit geometry such as warped point clouds or depth, which breaks down under large viewpoint changes. We present AnyCam, a method that represents the camera with an anchor object in the scene: we reconstruct it in 3D and render it along the target trajectory, a camera signal that is scale-aware, view-complete and easy to specify relative to the object. A video diffusion model transfers the content and dynamics of the source video to the new viewpoint. Its H-Concat layout aligns source and target frames in time, so the model can be distilled into AnyCam-AR, a streaming few-step generator for on-the-fly camera control. Both models are trained on paired videos with pixel-aligned anchor renderings from multi-camera videos and static-scene captures. Experiments on diverse datasets and trajectories show that AnyCam performs favorably against camera-controlled video generation and 3D reconstruction methods in camera control and visual quality.

title: Tracking Any Point with Agentic Visual Reasoning
abstract: A general-purpose Vision-Language Model (VLM) has surpassed expert vision models in many domains such as object detection and video recognition. However, point correspondence is known to be challenging for VLMs since it goes beyond object-level recognition: it requires pixel-level localization of the same physical surface point across observations, even when appearance changes or the point disappears and later reappears. In this paper, we introduce AgenTAP, a VLM-based agent that directly predicts point coordinates and visibility and actively reasons over videos. Starting from its own estimate, the agent autonomously chooses what to inspect and uses the resulting evidence to verify point identity and refine its predictions. With GPT-6 Astra, it surpasses expert vision models in both point localization and visibility prediction, without correspondence-specific fine-tuning. We further use AgenTAP to re-identify physical points after disappearance and reconnect fragmented tracks, constructing EgoTAP-4D, a dataset of 3D point trajectories in long real-world egocentric videos. On sampled reappearing points, its predictions approach human agreement, and adding EgoTAP-4D to D4RT training improves average 3D tracking performance.

title: Spectrum Adaptation of AI-Native Autoencoder Communications with Transfer Learning
abstract: End-to-end physical-layer learning replaces separate modulation, coding, and detection operations with an autoencoder (AE) that consists of a jointly trained encoder-decoder pair at the transmitter and the receiver. This paper studies AI-native communications with AEs and quantifies the sensitivity to training-test mismatch in channel models. Models trained only on an AWGN channel achieve low bit error rates (BERs) under matched conditions but degrade severely on Rayleigh fading with practical front-end impairments. To reduce the time and energy required to adapt to new channel conditions, we propose a low-latency transfer-learning procedure that starts from an AWGN-pretrained system and fine-tunes only a small subset of transmitter and receiver layers while freezing the remainder. We further formulate layer selection as a budget-constrained optimization problem that identifies the most informative parameters to update during adaptation. This preserves the learned signal geometry and the deep decision structure while adapting lightweight front ends to fading- and impairment-induced mixing. For AE communications, we show that partial updates remove the mismatch-induced error floor and approach the BER of fully retrained models. We provide a layer-wise study and quantify resource-performance trade-offs, showing that modest adaptation substantially reduces BER while cutting training time, multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations, energy consumption, and the fraction of updated parameters for resource-efficient implementation.

title: LuxAvatar: Real-Time Relightable Head Avatars via Causal Neural Shading of 3D Intrinsic Proxies
abstract: We present LuxAvatar, a feed-forward framework for real-time head avatar animation and relighting from a single portrait. To achieve both 3D controllability and complex facial light transport, we factorize avatar synthesis into an animatable 3D intrinsic Gaussian proxy and a causal autoregressive neural shader. This proxy disentangles canonical geometry and reflectance attributes, rapidly rasterizing deformed Gaussians into view- and motion-consistent PBR buffers. Conditioned on these buffers, our neural shader formulates forward rendering as a conditional video diffusion process, bypassing explicit PBR computation to synthesize realistic shading effects under target illumination. We achieve real-time streaming through heterogeneous distillation from a pretrained multi-step bidirectional relighting teacher to a two-step causal autoregressive neural shader, inheriting broad synthetic lighting priors while minimizing conditioning and decoding latency. To further specialize these priors to human heads, we construct a hybrid relighting dataset for domain-specific fine-tuning, capturing authentic facial dynamics and physically grounded light transport. Extensive experiments show that our framework enables 3D-controllable, real-time portrait animation and relighting, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in visual fidelity, motion control, and lighting accuracy.

title: Tokenisation is not in APX
abstract: In this paper, we prove that, unless P=NP, no polynomial-time algorithm can find a tokeniser whose objective is within any constant factor of the optimum, meaning that tokenisation is not in the APX complexity class. We prove this for direct and bottom-up tokenisation, under both a compression or unigram log-likelihood objectives, and for binary or larger alphabets. We further show that, even over unary alphabets, direct tokenisation is APX-hard, and thus admits no polynomial-time approximation scheme.

title: A Comparative Study of Artificial Intelligence Governance Patterns in Selected Countries
abstract: This study employs a comparative qualitative approach to analyze AI governance patterns in seven countries (Iran, the US, China, the EU, the UK, Japan, and Singapore). Data from official documents and academic sources were analyzed across five dimensions: policy focus, regulatory approach, ethical principles, technological infrastructure, and international cooperation. The findings identify three dominant patterns: 1) State-centered (China, Singapore), emphasizing central control and large-scale investment; 2) Market-based (US), relying on decentralized innovation and voluntary standards; and 3) Participatory-rights-based (EU, UK), featuring a risk-based approach with a focus on transparency and algorithmic justice. Japan focuses on solving social challenges through voluntary innovation. Despite institutional advances, Iran faces obstacles such as sanctions and structural inconsistencies. The conclusion underscores the need for a hybrid model tailored to Iran, integrating the EU's risk-based approach, Singapore's institutional coordination, and the localization of Islamic values. Policy recommendations include developing binding ethical codes, committing to long-term investment in indigenous infrastructure, and leading regional coalitions.

title: Can image generation help visual reasoning? An empirical study
abstract: Language models think in words; then multimodal models might think in images. We test whether a generated helper improves the answer to a visual question. A model describes the helper it needs and then answers using the original and generated images together. Across 13 vision-language model and generator pairs, generation lowers mean accuracy by 3.7 percentage points, with declines on nine of ten tasks. Two unified models, BAGEL and Janus-Pro-7B, each lose accuracy on eight tasks. On VSTAR, adding a generated image to the same planning hint lowers accuracy by 10.47 points. Repeated image edits yield different outcomes across tasks. ChartQAPro and MathVista stay below their no-generation baselines, while ERQA gains three points after ten edits.
